en: Thus have I heard: the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta, the 149th Discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the ‘Great Discourse on the Six Sense Bases.’”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it really is, not knowing and not seeing forms as they really are,
not knowing and not seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, not knowing and not seeing eye-contact as it really is—
whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— ”
Not knowing and not seeing that [eye] as it really is, one feels passion for the eye, one feels passion for forms,
one feels passion for eye-consciousness, one feels passion for eye-contact; and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—
whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— one feels passion for that as well.
As he dwells thus, infatuated, fettered, and deluded, contemplating gratification, the five aggregates of clinging increase in the future.
His craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there—increases.
Both his physical distresses and his mental distresses increase.
Bodily torments increase, and mental torments increase;
bodily fevers increase, and mental fevers increase.
He experiences both bodily suffering and mental suffering.
“Bhikkhus, not knowing and not seeing the ear as it really is …pe… not knowing and not seeing the nose as it really is …pe… not knowing and not seeing the tongue as it really is …pe…”

“Bhikkhus, not knowing and not seeing the body as it really is … [and so on] … not knowing and not seeing the mind as it really is, bhikkhus; not knowing and not seeing mental phenomena as they really are, bhikkhus;
not knowing and not seeing mind-consciousness as it really is, bhikkhus; not knowing and not seeing mind-contact as it really is, bhikkhus,” [the Blessed One said].
Not seeing as it really is, and not knowing as it really is, that feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— which arises conditioned by mental contact,

one becomes infatuated with the mind, infatuated with mental phenomena, infatuated with mental consciousness, and infatuated with mental contact, [namely] that which arises conditioned by mental contact.
A feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—and he becomes infatuated with it.
As he dwells infatuated, fettered, deluded, and contemplating gratification, the five aggregates of clinging increase for him in the future.
His craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there—increases within him.
His bodily distresses increase, and his mental distresses increase;
his bodily fevers increase, and his mental fevers increase; his bodily torments increase, and his mental torments increase.
Thus one experiences both bodily suffering and mental suffering.
But, monks, knowing and seeing the eye as it really is, knowing and seeing forms as they really are,
knowing and seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, and knowing and seeing eye-contact as it really is—
Whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by eye-contact,
knowing and seeing that as it truly is, one does not become infatuated with the eye, does not become infatuated with forms,
does not become infatuated with eye-consciousness, and does not become infatuated with eye-contact; whatever [feeling] arises conditioned by eye-contact...
Whether a feeling of pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure arises, he does not become infatuated with it.
As he dwells thus—without infatuation, without attachment, without delusion, and contemplating the danger—he brings about the diminution of the five aggregates of clinging in the future.
Furthermore, his craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there—is abandoned by him.
His physical distresses are abandoned, and his mental distresses are abandoned;
his physical fevers are abandoned, and his mental fevers are abandoned; his physical burning anxieties are abandoned, and his mental burning anxieties are abandoned.
Thus he experiences both bodily happiness and mental happiness.
The view he possesses in such a state is his right view;
the intention he possesses in such a state is his right intention.
The effort of one who has become such is his right effort;
the mindfulness of one who has become such is his right mindfulness;
the concentration of one who has become such is his right concentration.
Furthermore, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood have already been thoroughly purified.
In this way, this Noble Eightfold Path reaches fulfillment through development for him.
As he develops this Noble Eightfold Path in this manner, the four foundations of mindfulness also reach fulfillment through development.
They proceed; the four right endeavors reach fulfillment through development, the four bases of psychic power reach fulfillment through development,
the five faculties reach fulfillment through development,
the five powers reach fulfillment through development, and the seven factors of enlightenment reach fulfillment through development.
These two qualities proceed conjoined in him:
serenity and insight.
He fully understands with direct knowledge those phenomena that are to be fully understood through direct knowledge.
Those phenomena that are to be abandoned through direct knowledge, he abandons them through direct knowledge.
Those phenomena that are to be developed through direct knowledge, he develops them through direct knowledge.
Those phenomena that are to be realized through direct knowledge, he realizes them through direct knowledge.
"And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena to be fully understood through direct knowledge?

It should be said: 'The five aggregates of clinging,' namely—the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to volitional formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness."
These phenomena are to be fully understood through direct knowledge.
And what, monks, are the phenomena to be abandoned through direct knowledge?
Ignorance and craving for existence.
These phenomena are to be abandoned through direct knowledge.
And what, monks, are the phenomena to be developed through direct knowledge?
Tranquility and insight.
These things are to be developed through direct knowledge.
And what, monks, are the things to be realized through direct knowledge?
Knowledge and liberation.
These phenomena are to be realized through direct knowledge. Monks,
knowing and seeing the ear as it really is … [and so on] … monks,
knowing and seeing the nose as it really is … [and so on].
Monks, knowing and seeing the tongue as it really is …pe… monks,
knowing and seeing the body as it really is …pe… monks,
knowing and seeing the mind as it really is, knowing and seeing mental phenomena as they really are, and knowing and seeing mind-consciousness as it really is.
Knowing and seeing mental contact as it really is, knowing and seeing mental contact as it really is,
and knowing and seeing as it really is that feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—

that arises conditioned by mental contact, one does not become infatuated with the mind, does not become infatuated with mental phenomena, does not become infatuated with mental consciousness, nor with mental contact.
One does not become attached; one does not become attached even to that feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by mental contact.
For one who dwells thus unattached, unbound, undeluded, and contemplating the danger [of suffering], the five aggregates of clinging will in the future come to their diminution.
His craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there—is abandoned by him.
His physical distresses are abandoned, and his mental distresses are abandoned;
his physical fevers are abandoned, and his mental fevers are abandoned.
The feverish distresses of the body are abandoned, and the feverish distresses of the mind are also abandoned.
He experiences both bodily happiness and mental happiness.
The view held by one who has become thus is his right view.
Whatever intention belongs to one who has become such is right intention for him;
whatever effort belongs to one who has become such is right effort for him;
whatever mindfulness belongs to one who has become such is right mindfulness for him.
The concentration of one who has become thus is his right concentration.
Furthermore, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood have already been completely purified beforehand.
In this way, this noble eightfold path reaches fulfillment through development.
As he thus develops this Noble Eightfold Path, the four foundations of mindfulness reach the fulfillment of their development;
the four right efforts reach the fulfillment of their development; the four bases of psychic power reach the fulfillment of their development;
and the five faculties reach the fulfillment of their development. The five...
The powers reach fulfillment through development, and the seven factors of enlightenment also reach fulfillment through development.
These two qualities proceed conjoined in him:
serenity and insight.
Thus, those phenomena that are to be fully understood through direct knowledge, he fully understands them through direct knowledge;
those phenomena that are to be abandoned through direct knowledge, he abandons them through direct knowledge;
those phenomena that are to be developed through direct knowledge, he develops them through direct knowledge.
He realizes through direct knowledge those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
And what, bhikkhus, are the states to be fully understood through direct knowledge?

“The five aggregates of clinging,” it should be said; that is to say: [the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness].

The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
These phenomena are to be fully understood through direct knowledge.
And what, monks, are the phenomena to be abandoned through direct knowledge?
Ignorance and craving for existence—
these phenomena are to be abandoned through direct knowledge.
And what, monks, are the phenomena to be developed through direct knowledge?
Calm and insight—
these phenomena are to be developed through direct knowledge.
And what, monks, are the phenomena to be realized through direct knowledge?
“Knowledge and liberation—
these are the phenomena to be realized through direct higher knowledge.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta, the seventh, is finished.
